title: Freya and the Orchard
premise: Mirabel Galloway, a wedding planner who stopped believing in love after orchestrating his own parents' bitter divorce proceedings disguised as a remarriage, inherits a third of a failing cider orchard in rural Aldercombe — the other two-thirds belonging to Freya Lindqvist, the childhood friend he abandoned fifteen years ago to survive. Forced into an uneasy co-ownership, Mirabel plans one final wedding on the orchard grounds while Freya fights to keep the land from a developer's grasp, and their old wound becomes the very thing that might save both the trees and each other. When the orchard's fate is decided at a town auction, Mirabel must publicly choose between the invisible, contained life he built and the person who once knew him completely. He stays past the last train, signs the deed over to Freya and the town trust, and lets himself be known — the orchard survives, and so, finally, does he.
about_author: Petra Reyes is a former estate lawyer who spent a decade untangling inherited property disputes before turning to fiction about the families they leave behind. She writes from a converted barn in the Hudson Valley, where she keeps a scruffy orchard of her own.

chapters.title: The Muscle That Learns
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In London, Mirabel flawlessly executes his two-hundredth wedding, then receives a solicitor's letter: a deceased great-aunt has left him a third share of an orchard deed co-signed by Freya Lindqvist — a name he buried fifteen years ago. Emotional beat: controlled detachment cracking at the first sight of her name.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Tree
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya, running the struggling orchard alone since her father's death, learns a stranger holds two-thirds of her land and assumes it's a developer's trick — until Mirabel steps off the train. Their reunion is frost over old fire. Emotional beat: guarded hostility masking grief at being left behind.

chapters.title: Terms of Coexistence
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Legal deadlock forces an arrangement: Mirabel will stay one month to help stage a society wedding on the grounds — revenue Freya desperately needs — while she teaches him the orchard. He tells himself proximity means nothing. Emotional beat: the dangerous comfort of a shared routine re-forming.

chapters.title: What the Frost Took
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A late frost threatens the blossom and the wedding contract with it; working through the night with smudge pots, they fall into old rhythms, and Freya glimpses the boy Mirabel was before he learned to disappear. Emotional beat: reluctant tenderness, and the first crack in Mirabel's armor.

chapters.title: The Client Who Wanted Everything
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The bride demands the orchard be 'perfected' — old trees felled for a glass marquee. Mirabel, professionally obliged, begins drafting the removal plan and realizes he's once again the man who arranges beautiful things for people who don't care what they cost. Emotional beat: complicity and self-disgust.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Silence, Explained Badly
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya confronts him about why he vanished after the night everything changed between them as teenagers. Mirabel deflects with a half-truth about his family's ruin, and Freya, hurt again, tells him the developer's offer is real — and that she may have to take it. Emotional beat: rupture; the wound reopened deliberately.

chapters.title: The Last Train Schedule
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. His month ends; the wedding is a triumph, the client delighted, his old life waiting. At the station he holds a one-way ticket and Freya's hand-drawn map of the orchard, every tree named, including the one they climbed as children. Emotional beat: the full weight of choosing invisibility made physical.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The developer forces the co-owners' dispute to a town auction of the disputed share. Freya stands to lose everything until Mirabel arrives mid-bidding and does the unthinkable: he publicly tells the truth of why he left — his father's crimes, his shame — and pledges his share to the town land trust. Emotional beat: climax; exposure as salvation.

chapters.title: After the Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The developer withdraws; the orchard is saved as a community trust with Freya as steward. Mirabel, having missed his train on purpose, asks not for a share of the deed but for a place to stay and work. Freya's answer is a second mug of cider and the spare key. Emotional beat: quiet, terrified hope.

chapters.title: First Blossom
chapters.summary: Shared POV, alternating. Spring: the trees bloom over the saved orchard as the town gathers for a small, unofficial wedding — not one Mirabel planned, but one he's simply in. He lets Freya read the letter he wrote at fifteen and never sent. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, not inherited; the heart, trained at last to stay.
